name: AD620ARZ-REEL
title: Instrumentation amplifier, 1.3 mA, gain 1 to 10,000 from one resistor
summary: The AD620 is a single-chip in-amp whose gain, from 1 to 10,000, is set by a single resistor between pins 1 and 8. It runs from ±2.3 V to ±18 V on 1.3 mA maximum and has a Superbeta bipolar input pair for low bias current and 9 nV/√Hz noise. A and B grades cover −40 °C to +85 °C in PDIP and SOIC, the S grade −55 °C to +125 °C in CERDIP; the A grade is also sold as bare die. Typical uses are bridge and pressure sensors, weigh scales, ECG and other medical inputs, and battery-powered data acquisition.
key_figures: 9 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz; 0.28 μV p-p, 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz

circuits.title: Settling time test circuit
circuits.description: A 10 V p-p input feeds the inverting input through 100 kΩ. A selector switch either shorts the 100 kΩ (G = 1) or ties the inverting input to ground through 11 kΩ, 1 kΩ or 100 Ω (G = 10, 100, 1000). A second switch puts 5.49 kΩ, 499 Ω or 49.9 Ω across the RG pins, or leaves them open for G = 1. The non-inverting input and REF go to ground. A 10 kΩ resistor from the input, a 1 kΩ ten-turn trimmer and a 10 kΩ resistor from the output form a chain; the trimmer wiper is VOUT.

parts.note: common COM; positions G1, G10, G100, G1000
common COM; positions G1 (open), G10, G100, G1000

notes: All resistors are 1 % tolerance.

circuits.title: Bridge transducer amplifier, G = 100 (make vs. buy)
circuits.description: A bridge of four 350 Ω strain-gauge arms excited from 10 V gives a 20 mV full-scale differential signal. An AD620A with RG = 499 Ω (G = 100) amplifies it, its REF pin grounded; supply current is 1.3 mA maximum. The error budget table works through this circuit.
notes: Error budget conditions: VS = ±15 V.

circuits.title: Pressure monitor on a single 5 V supply
circuits.description: A 3 kΩ pressure transducer bridge runs from 5 V and draws 1.7 mA. Its two outputs drive an AD620B set to G = 100 by a 499 Ω RG, powered from 5 V and ground. A 20 kΩ / 10 kΩ / 20 kΩ string across the supply makes two taps: the upper one is the ADC reference, the lower one is buffered by an AD705 follower whose output drives the AD620 REF pin and the ADC analog ground. Currents: AD620 1.3 mA max, divider 0.10 mA, AD705 0.6 mA max; 3.8 mA in all.
notes: The ADC's own supply connections are not drawn.

circuits.title: Medical ECG monitor front end
circuits.description: Two body electrodes reach the AD620A inputs through a patient protection and isolation barrier. RG is 8.25 kΩ in parallel with two 24.9 kΩ resistors in series (R3, R2); the in-amp runs at G = 7. The junction of R3 and R2 goes to the inverting input of an AD705J whose non-inverting input is grounded; its feedback is R4 (1 MΩ) in parallel with C1 in series with R1 (10 kΩ). The AD705J output drives the third, right-leg electrode. C1 is chosen for stability of this right-leg drive loop. Two 3 V cells give ±3 V; REF is grounded. The output passes a 0.03 Hz high-pass filter and an output amplifier of gain 143, for 1 V/mV overall. Isolation is required to protect the patient.

parts.note: value chosen for right-leg drive loop stability

notes: The AD705J supply pins are not shown.

circuits.title: Precision voltage-to-current converter
circuits.description: The AD620 output voltage VX appears across R1 and becomes the load current. An AD705 follower senses the load end of R1 and drives REF, which keeps CMR high; the current into the load is VX/R1, less the op amp's input bias current. The circuit runs on 1.8 mA from ±3 V.

circuits.title: Diode protection for inputs beyond the supplies
circuits.description: Each input has a series resistor R and a pair of low-leakage diodes from the input pin to the two supplies, so a source that swings past a rail is clamped and its current is limited by R. REF is grounded.

circuits.title: Input filter against RF interference
circuits.description: Each input is fed through a resistor R with a capacitor CC to ground; a capacitor CD sits across the two inputs. CD sets the differential bandwidth, the CC pair the common-mode bandwidth; CD is at least ten times CC so that a mismatch between the two R·CC products costs little CMR. RG is 499 Ω (G = 100). Each supply is decoupled with 0.1 μF and 10 μF to ground.

circuits.title: Differential shield driver
circuits.description: Each input arrives on its own shielded cable. The two halves of an AD648 dual op amp follow the voltages on the two RG pins, and each drives one cable's shield through 100 Ω, bootstrapping the cable capacitance. Each op amp has a diode from its output to its inverting input and a resistor from that input to −VS.

parts.note: dual op amp, halves A and B

notes: The AD648's own supply pins are not drawn.

circuits.title: Common-mode shield driver
circuits.description: RG is split into two equal halves; their midpoint carries the input common-mode voltage. An AD548 follower buffers it and drives the shield of the input cable through 100 Ω, so the shield moves with the common-mode signal.
notes: The AD548's own supply pins are not drawn.

circuits.title: Ground return for bias currents, transformer-coupled input
circuits.description: A transformer's secondary drives the two inputs; its centre tap is tied to the power supply ground, which is the DC path the input bias currents need. REF and the load return to the same ground.

parts.note: primary P1, P2; secondary S1, S2 with centre tap CT

circuits.title: Ground return for bias currents, thermocouple input
circuits.description: A thermocouple feeds the two inputs; its lead on +IN is also tied to the power supply ground to return the bias currents. REF and the load return to the same ground.

circuits.title: Ground return for bias currents, AC-coupled input
circuits.description: An AC source reaches the inputs through series capacitors; a 100 kΩ resistor from each input to the power supply ground gives the bias currents their DC path. REF and the load return to the same ground.

circuits.title: Basic grounding practice
circuits.description: An AD620 feeds an AD585 sample-and-hold, which feeds an AD574A ADC. An analog supply (+15 V, common, −15 V) powers all three; a digital supply (+5 V, common) powers the ADC logic. Each IC's supplies are decoupled: 0.1 µF from each AD620 and AD585 supply to a midpoint, 1 µF across the ADC supplies. The AD620 REF pin, the AD585 pin 6, both decoupling midpoints, the analog common and the digital common each return on their own wire to the AD574A analog common, pin 9, which is joined to its digital common, pin 15.

operation.text: The AD620 is a monolithic in-amp derived from the three-op-amp topology. Its input is a single bipolar differential pair, Q1 and Q2, made with Superbeta transistors that cut input bias current by about ten times. Two feedback loops (Q1-A1-R1 and Q2-A2-R2) hold the collector currents of the input pair constant, which forces the differential input voltage across RG. A unity-gain difference amplifier, A3, built with four 10 kΩ resistors, removes the common-mode part and gives one output referred to REF. Each input has a 400 Ω series resistor and ESD diodes; each input stage runs at 20 μA.

operation.topic: Effect of RG on the input stage
operation.text: RG also sets the preamp transconductance, which approaches that of the input transistors as RG gets smaller at higher gain. As gain is raised, open-loop gain grows and gain errors shrink; the gain-bandwidth product, fixed by C1, C2 and the preamp transconductance, grows; and input voltage noise falls to 9 nV/√Hz, set mainly by the input transistors' collector current and base resistance.

Gain is set by the impedance between pins 1 and 8. The internal resistors are laser trimmed to an absolute 24.7 kΩ, so one external resistor sets the gain accurately (0.15 % at G = 100) with 0.1 % to 1 % parts. For G = 1 the RG pins stay open. Resistance in series with RG adds gain error; RG's temperature coefficient adds gain drift, and below 10 ppm/°C is best.
Offset has an input part and an output part. Referred to the input, the output part is divided by the gain, so input offset dominates at high gain and output offset at low gain.

The voltage on REF is the output's zero. It is useful when the load's ground differs from the system ground, and it lets a precise offset be added to the output; REF can range to within 2 V of either supply. Series resistance at REF degrades CMR, so it is kept small and REF is driven from a low impedance.

The inputs survive ±60 mA for several hours at room temperature, at any gain, with the part powered or unpowered. For long-term exposure the input current stays at or below 6 mA. When an input can go past the supplies, a series resistor in each input limits the current to 6 mA; it can double as the RFI filter resistor. Large resistors cost noise and AC CMRR. Low-leakage clamp diodes at the inputs (such as BAV199) reduce the resistance needed.

An in-amp turns small signals above its bandwidth into a small DC offset. A low-pass RC network at the inputs removes them. CD acts on the difference signal and CC on the common-mode signal; any mismatch between the R·CC products degrades CMRR, so CC is kept at least ten times smaller than CD, and raising the CD:CC ratio makes CC mismatch matter less.

For best CMR, REF goes to a low-impedance point and the resistance and capacitance seen by the two inputs are matched. With shielded input cables, driving the shields from the signal (a differential or a common-mode shield driver) bootstraps the cable capacitance and keeps CMR up at higher frequencies.

Because the output is developed relative to REF, tying REF to the right local ground removes many grounding problems. In a mixed-signal system, ground current in shared wires and traces can cause errors of hundreds of millivolts; analog and digital grounds return separately and join at one point, usually at the ADC.

The input transistors need a DC path for their bias currents. A floating source (a transformer, a thermocouple, an AC-coupled source) must have, for each input, a DC route to ground: a grounded centre tap, a grounded lead, or a resistor from each input to ground.

The die has two pads at each RG node. To keep bond-wire resistance out of the gain, RG is wired as a Kelvin connection: pads 1A and 1B are joined at one RG terminal, pads 8A and 8B at the other. For G = 1 with no RG, 1A is bonded to 1B and 8A to 8B.

For a 20 mV full-scale bridge at G = 100 over −40 °C to +85 °C, the AD620A circuit totals 14,663 ppm of full scale against 28,134 ppm for a three-op-amp design built from OP07D parts, and draws 1.3 mA maximum against 15 mA. Absolute accuracy and drift dominate in simple systems; where a processor runs an autogain/autozero cycle, only gain, nonlinearity and noise remain, which allows 14-bit accuracy.
The part suits higher-resistance pressure sensors run from low voltages, and voltage-output pressure transducers. In the 5 V circuit the 3 kΩ bridge draws 1.7 mA and the whole signal chain 3.8 mA.

Low current noise suits ECG electrodes, whose source resistance can be 1 MΩ or more. In the ECG circuit C1 sets the stability of the right-leg drive loop, and the patient must be protected by isolation.
Input offset voltage shifts by about 0.5 μV in the first two minutes after power is applied, then holds.
